title: Personal Project Moderation: A Student Guide
summary: Personal Project moderation explained for MYP Year 5 students. Learn how teacher marks are checked, samples are reviewed, and final grades are protected.
body_markdown:
Finishing an MYP Personal Project can feel final. You submit the report, look once more at the product that consumed months of planning, and wait. Yet another stage remains: **Personal Project moderation** .


Your supervisor assesses your report using the MYP criteria, and the IB reviews a sample of your school's assessed work. This external check determines whether the school has applied the expected international standard. For students, the practical priority is clear: make your evidence understandable to a reader outside your school.


### Personal Project moderation at a glance


Here is the journey your work takes:


- You complete your product and submit your report.
- Your supervisor assesses the report against the MYP criteria.
- The school checks that teachers have interpreted the criteria consistently.
- An external examiner reviews a sample of assessed work.
- Marks may be confirmed or adjusted before the final grade is determined.


Revisit the project's purpose and components in RevisionDojo's[MYP Personal Project overview](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/what-is-the-myp-personal-project) .


### The report makes your learning visible


Consider Maya, a hypothetical Year 5 student designing a balcony garden for pollinating insects. Her learning goal concerns suitable planting; her product is a garden model with a seasonal planting guide.


The model is the most visible outcome. However, her report must communicate what the model cannot: how she established her goal, planned the work, applied approaches to learning (ATL) skills, and evaluated the result.


A polished product cannot compensate for missing explanations. Equally, a product with limitations can support meaningful reflection when Maya evaluates it honestly against suitable success criteria. The report gives the assessor evidence of the thinking behind the outcome.


A student protects a tiny bridge in a museum case while a teacher points to the project report


### The supervisor marks the report first


Assessment begins inside the school. Maya's supervisor applies the published criteria to her report, rather than awarding marks for effort or comparison with classmates.


The structure uses three criteria, each worth up to 8 marks:


Criterion What Maya needs to demonstrate


A: Planning A learning goal, intended product, appropriate success criteria, and a plan


B: Applying skills How ATL skills supported the learning goal and product


C: Reflecting The impact on her learning and evaluation against the product's success criteria


Together, these produce a maximum of 24 marks. The[Personal Project criteria guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/myp-personal-project-criteria) explains the descriptors, while the[Personal Project grading guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-is-the-myp-personal-project-graded) distinguishes criterion marks from the final grade.


If Maya simply writes that she used research skills, the assessor has little evidence. A stronger explanation shows how she compared horticultural sources, checked local climate conditions, and changed plant selections after discovering unsuitable flowering seasons. That connects the skill to an action and its effect.


### The school checks marking consistency


When several supervisors assess projects, they need a shared interpretation of the descriptors. Teachers may compare examples, discuss differences, and agree how the criteria apply. This process is often called internal standardization.


Its purpose is fairness: equivalent evidence should receive equivalent marks regardless of the supervisor. Consistency also helps the school explain and support the judgments submitted for external moderation.


Supervisors guide students without becoming co-authors. The[guide to the Personal Project supervisor's role](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/role-of-the-myp-personal-project-supervisor) explains those boundaries. Maya remains responsible for her decisions, work, and explanations.


### The IB reviews a sample


All MYP Year 5 students are registered for external moderation of the Personal Project. This does not mean an examiner independently remarks every report. The examiner reviews a sample of work already assessed by the school to check its marking standard.


Think of this as checking a measuring instrument's calibration. The examiner considers whether the awarded marks are supported by the evidence and descriptors. Maya's garden is assessed against the same criteria as a different student's podcast.


If the school's marking matches the expected standard, marks can be confirmed. If its interpretation is too generous or severe, moderation can lead to adjustments. These may affect students whose reports were outside the sample because the process checks the school's assessment standard.


Students therefore cannot prepare differently depending on sample selection. The useful approach is to make every report clear enough for an informed external reader.


### Check the evidence before submission


An examiner can assess submitted evidence, not memories of what happened. A useful conversation or prototype change needs an explanation showing how it demonstrates the criterion.


Before submitting, Maya checks:


- Does each important claim include a concrete example?
- Does she explain how ATL skills affected her learning or product?
- Does she evaluate each success criterion with evidence?
- Does reflection explain learning rather than merely recount events?
- Are sources acknowledged appropriately?


RevisionDojo's[Personal Project report guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/how-to-write-myp-personal-project-report) supports this structural check. Its guide to[common Personal Project mistakes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/common-myp-personal-project-mistakes) helps identify gaps. AI Chat and grading tools can support practice and questioning, subject to school rules on AI use, acknowledgment, and student authorship.


### Prepare for the standard


Moderation does not automatically reward expensive materials, hours worked, or elaborate products. Students creating very different outcomes can demonstrate equivalent achievement through planning, applying skills, and reflection.


Maya's strongest preparation is a report that makes her decisions and learning visible. A sample report can help her understand effective evidence, but her explanations must remain her own.


RevisionDojo brings support together through its Coursework Library, Study Notes, Flashcards, AI Chat, grading tools, and Tutors. As students progress into later IB study, its Questionbank, Predicted Papers, and Mock Exams support the same habit of practising against clear expectations.


After months of independent work, moderation can feel like another uncertainty. Understanding its purpose makes the next step clearer: present evidence carefully, follow your school's requirements, and let the report show what you learned.
